tagline: Follow the Arkansas beneath high peaks, through towns shaped by mining.
intro: The Collegiate Peaks Byway follows the foot of the Sawatch Range on 57 miles of paved road, much of it beside the Arkansas River. Colorado DOT gives a driving time of 90 minutes and emphasizes the contrast between high peaks, riverside stretches, working ranches and natural hot springs. It is a Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway, following the upper Arkansas past eight of the Rocky Mountains’ highest peaks. Side trips reach the mining towns of Vicksburg, Winfield and St. Elmo; aquamarine, Colorado’s state gemstone, is mined on Mount Antero.

By 1877, the Leadville Stagecoach Road ran through Granite, carrying supplies and mail as well as passengers. Traces of that earlier road remain, while Highway 24 runs on the river’s west side. Farther south, the link between Buena Vista and Poncha Springs was designated US 650 in 1926, before US 285 was commissioned in 1936. The stage road through Granite survives as a hiking and cycling trail.

Start at Granite on the Arkansas, between the Mosquito and Sawatch ranges, and head south toward Buena Vista. At Nathrop, Chalk Creek meets the Arkansas beneath the valley of Mount Princeton and Mount Antero. Continue to Salida, named for the river’s exit from the valley into Bighorn Sheep Canyon.

moments.title: Granite
moments.text: Heaps of rounded granite boulders along the Arkansas mark the work of placer miners. They used sluice boxes to separate heavy gold flakes from gravel washed along by the current. After gold was found in Low Pass Gulch in 1867, Granite drew miners from nearby Cache Creek. Prospecting later moved into the hills in search of gold-bearing veins; old hard-rock mining tunnels remain there. As the ore diminished, the town’s population declined. The old Colorado Midland grade is also visible in Granite, another trace of the valley’s work of moving ore and supplies.

moments.title: Buena Vista
moments.text: Buildings from the 1880s and 1890s remain in Buena Vista, a town that grew with three railroads serving silver, gold and lead mines. Water also supported agriculture in the valley, helping its economy withstand mining’s cycles of expansion and decline. The town stands below Mount Princeton, Mount Yale, Mount Columbia and Mount Harvard. Several peaks take their names from universities, giving this part of the Sawatch Range its collective name. Alsina Dearheimer chose the town’s Spanish name, meaning “Good View,” and specified its Americanized pronunciation when residents selected it at incorporation.

moments.title: Mount Antero
moments.text: Aquamarine is mined on Mount Antero, and active private mining claims extend onto surrounding peaks. The mountain is named for Chief Antero of the Uintah band of the Ute people. It rises south of Mount Princeton in the San Isabel National Forest. One climbing route starts near St. Elmo and follows a forest road up Baldwin Creek toward the summit. That route carries heavy mining and tourist traffic during fair summer weather. Another hiking route begins at Browns Creek Trailhead, follows Little Browns Creek and joins Forest Road 1A high on the mountain.
